name: Dr. Cressida Lilyapen, a botanist named after the delicately perfumed hybrid she cultivated thirteen years before her sensibilities were touched by the tangible grace of blooming things. Her hair shines with dye that changes color at noon. Her eyes close less than those of others, she thinks, as she talks with plants. Her fingers smell of dried blossoms, even on washday. She sits like a cross between a patient and an informer as the commuters around her drift by without knowing her silent grief until, finally, she walks toward the open fields on sunny afternoons, her thinness wavering in a way that is said to be elegant, her blue robes almost translucent in the sunlight, the collar folded over to show a bit of soft flesh. Drunk on the air of strangers outside her own backyard, she weeps quietly under the shade of a tree where she can also see a man staring at another girl in a park with a camera rolled up gleaming in the wind. She sighs, tears some myrtle and phlox, ties the bundle with craft cord she bought after racking up her first hundred-dollar deficit, and now live without shoes, wearing fuzzy socks instead. Her dead mother has smothered her grandmother, Cressida’s emotions swirl helplessly until, one day, she drifts out of reach of her own chair to rest on a bed of buttercups and realize there is nothing to keep her where she is for more minutes yet
